01.note: A man leading the prayers in front of Rabbi Ḥanina stretched out the opening praise of God, calling Him the great, the mighty, the awesome, the powerful, the strong and the fearless. Rabbi Ḥanina asked him whether he had now finished all the praises of his Master. Even the three standard words, he said, we would not dare to say had Moses not written them in the Torah and the Great Assembly not placed them in the prayer. Piling on more is like praising a man who owns countless thousands of gold coins for owning a thousand silver ones: it insults him.
01.why: The mishna rules that a prayer leader who adds improper wording is silenced, and just before this a leader in front of Rabba added pleas to God's mercy. This is a second case of a leader who added his own words to the fixed prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage in whose presence the man led the prayers, and who rebuked him for adding praises.

terms.meaning: Led the congregation in prayer; the prayer leader stood in front of the ark holding the Torah scrolls.
The central prayer of every service, said standing, which opens with praises of God.
The body of Sages that, by tradition, fixed the wording of the prayers.
A coin; gold dinars were worth far more than silver ones.

02.note: A man was reading the prophetic portion in the synagogue in front of Rabbi Eliezer, and he read Ezekiel's chapter that opens: Make known to Jerusalem her abominations. Rabbi Eliezer said to him: before you examine the abominations of Jerusalem, go and examine the abominations of your own mother. They looked into the man's lineage and found a stain of illegitimacy in it.
02.why: The Gemara is going through a list of sensitive Bible passages and whether each may be read and translated aloud in synagogue. The list allows this chapter of Ezekiel, and the story shows that Rabbi Eliezer held otherwise, the view the list sets aside.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who objected when a man read Ezekiel's rebuke of Jerusalem in his presence.

terms.meaning: A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.
A reading from the Prophets that follows the Torah reading in synagogue.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
A flaw in a person's family line, here because his mother had a forbidden sexual relationship.

03.note: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel came to the village of Kavul, where the synagogue sexton was reading aloud the verse telling how Reuben lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, while a translator rendered the reading for the congregation. Rabbi Ḥanina told the translator to stop and translate only the end of the verse. The Sages praised him for it.
03.why: The Gemara is listing passages that are read aloud in synagogue but not translated for the listeners, and the story of Reuben comes first on that list. Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel's instruction shows the rule being applied.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel
people.about: A Sage visiting Kavul who stopped the translator from translating the verse about Reuben.

people.name: Reuben
people.about: Son of Jacob, the subject of the verse being read.

people.name: Bilhah
people.about: His father's concubine, named in the verse.

terms.meaning: In the synagogue each verse of the Torah was read in Hebrew and then translated aloud into the language the people spoke.
The synagogue attendant, here the one reading from the Torah.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often expanding on it.

04.note: Rabbi Yehuda reported that the bronze workers in Jerusalem had a synagogue of their own, which they sold to Rabbi Eliezer, and he used it for all his own needs. The Gemara asks how they could sell it, since Jerusalem is a city, and answers that it was a small synagogue that the bronze workers had built themselves.
04.why: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, citing Rabbi Yonatan, has just ruled that a village synagogue may be sold but a city synagogue may not, because people from outside use it. This sale in Jerusalem is raised as an objection to that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who bought the bronze workers' synagogue and used it for his own needs.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
The Gemara cites an earlier source that seems to contradict a ruling just given.

05.note: A synagogue of the Jews of Rome opened onto a room where a corpse lay, so the impurity of the dead spread into the synagogue, and the priests, who may not be under the same roof as a corpse, could not go in to pray. They came to Rava. He told them to lift the synagogue's ark and set it down in the doorway between the rooms: a wooden object made to stay in one place cannot itself become impure, so it blocks impurity from passing. His colleagues go on to challenge this solution in the discussion that follows.
05.why: Rava has just given a run of rulings on the holiness of the ark and its fittings; here he uses the ark itself as a practical barrier. The Rabbis then object that an ark is sometimes moved with a scroll inside, and Rava concedes there is then no remedy.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage the priests consulted, who told them to use the ark as a barrier.

terms.meaning: A state of impurity spread by a dead body to people and objects under the same roof; priests are forbidden to contract it.
The cabinet in which a synagogue's Torah scrolls are kept.
A wooden object made to stay put, which the law treats as unable to become impure, so it can act as a barrier.

05.flag: The STORY stops at Rava's instruction; the Rabbis' objection and Rava's admission that no remedy is possible (AFTER segment 5) read as the end of the same incident.

06.note: Rav Huna declared a fast day, and Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai came to him with all the people of his town. They were asked to give charity and they gave. When they were ready to go home, they asked Rav Huna to hand the money back so they could support the poor of their own town. Rav Huna answered with a teaching: the money goes home with visitors only where the town has no town scholar; where there is one, it is given to him. All the more so here, he said, since both his poor and theirs rely on him.
06.why: Rabbi Yoḥanan, citing Rabbi Meir, has ruled that visitors who pledge charity in another town take the money home for their own poor, and a baraita confirms it. Rav Huna's case marks a limit to that ruling.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who declared the fast and kept the charity collected from the visitors.

people.name: Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai
people.about: He came with the people of his town and asked for their charity back.

terms.meaning: A day of public fasting and prayer declared in a time of trouble, when charity was also collected.
A Torah scholar who oversees a community's affairs, including how its charity is used.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

06.flag: Segment 4 is the baraita stating the general rule, not part of the Rav Huna incident; the story proper begins at segment 5.

07.note: Rav Huna once stood before Rav with a piece of straw tied around him for a belt. Rav asked what this was. Rav Huna said he had had no wine to sanctify the Sabbath day, so he pawned his belt and bought wine with it. Rav said: may it be God's will that you be wrapped in silk. Later, at the wedding of Rav Huna's son Rabba, Rav Huna, a short man, was lying on a bed, and his daughters and daughters-in-law came in and threw their silk garments on him until he was wrapped in silk. When Rav heard, he was angry: why, when I blessed you, did you not answer, And likewise to the Master?
07.why: The Gemara is recounting how Sages explained their long lives. Rabbi Zakkai credited his care never to miss sanctifying the Sabbath over wine, even when his mother sold her kerchief to buy it; Rav Huna's sacrifice for the same mitzva, and its reward, follow.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: He pawned his belt to buy wine for the Sabbath blessing and was later covered in silk.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who blessed Rav Huna that he be wrapped in silk.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, at whose wedding the blessing came true.

terms.meaning: The blessing over wine said at the start of the Sabbath, known as kiddush.
A customary reply to a blessing, wishing the same good on the one who gave it.

08.note: Rav Huna was walking home with a hoe on his shoulder. Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai came and, out of respect for his teacher, took it from him to carry it himself. Rav Huna said: if you are used to carrying such things in your own town, carry it; if not, I do not want to be honored through your degradation.
08.why: Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana said he earned long life partly because he never gained honor through another's degradation. The Gemara offers Rav Huna's refusal as an example of what that means.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage carrying his own hoe, who would not let his student carry it for him if that would shame the student.

people.name: Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai
people.about: Rav Huna's student, who offered to carry the hoe.

09.note: Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Neḥunya the Great in what merit he had lived so long. Rabbi Neḥunya's attendants came and began beating Rabbi Akiva, and he climbed up and sat at the top of a date palm. From there he asked a question about the daily offering: if the verse says lamb, why does it also say one? Rabbi Neḥunya told his attendants: he is a young Torah scholar, let him be. He then answered that one means the finest of its flock. His answer to the first question comes next in the discussion.
09.why: The Gemara is collecting Sages' answers to the question of how they earned long life; this is one more such asking, and Rabbi Neḥunya's own list of merits follows straight after.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: He asked Rabbi Neḥunya about his long life, was beaten by the attendants, and won his hearing with a Torah question.

people.name: Rabbi Neḥunya the Great
people.about: The elderly Sage whom Rabbi Akiva questioned.

terms.meaning: The lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and afternoon, described in Numbers 28.
A promising student of Torah; recognizing Rabbi Akiva as one, Rabbi Neḥunya had him spared.

09.flag: Rabbi Neḥunya's answer to the longevity question, the point of the episode, is in AFTER segment 6, outside the STORY.

10.note: Reish Lakish was traveling and came to a deep puddle; a man came along, lifted him onto his shoulders and began carrying him across. Reish Lakish asked whether he had read the Bible; he had. Had he studied Mishna? Four of its orders, the man said. Reish Lakish said: you have hewn four mountains and you carry the son of Lakish on your shoulders? Throw the son of Lakish into the water. The man said he was glad to serve the Master. Then, said Reish Lakish, learn from me this teaching of Rabbi Zeira: Jewish women took on themselves to wait seven clean days even for a spot of blood the size of a mustard seed.
10.why: Reish Lakish taught that one who makes use of a person who studies halakha will perish, and Ulla said one may be served by someone who studies four orders of Mishna but not by one who teaches them. The story shows Reish Lakish living by his own rule.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who refused to be carried by a learned man until he had taught him something.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage whose saying introduces the story.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Reish Lakish passed on to the man.

terms.meaning: The early compilation of Jewish law, divided into six orders, or large sections.
The days a woman counts without any sign of blood after her period before immersing in a ritual bath.
Reish Lakish speaking of himself by his family name.

11.note: Abaye said that in Babylonia the Divine Presence rests at times in the ancient synagogue of Huzal and at times in the synagogue that was destroyed and rebuilt in Neharde'a, and that whenever he was within a parasang of one, he went in to pray there. Once the father of Shmuel and Levi were sitting in the Neharde'a synagogue when the Divine Presence came; they heard a loud sound, rose and left. Another time Rav Sheshet was sitting there when the Divine Presence came, and he did not leave. The ministering angels came and frightened him. He said before God: when one is wretched and the other is not, who should give way to whom? God said to the angels: leave him.
11.why: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai has just taught that the Divine Presence went with the Jewish people into every exile, Babylonia included. The Gemara asks where in Babylonia it rests, and these accounts answer.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who named the two synagogues and made a point of praying in them.

people.name: the father of Shmuel
people.about: He left the synagogue when the Divine Presence came.

people.name: Levi
people.about: He left the synagogue with Shmuel's father.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who stayed when the Divine Presence came; the translation explains he was blind.

people.name: God
people.about: He told the angels to leave Rav Sheshet alone.

terms.meaning: God's presence as felt dwelling in a particular place.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles.
The angels who serve before God.

12.note: Ravina and Rabba Tosefa'a were walking along the road and saw a man drawing water with a bucket during the intermediate days of a Festival. Rabba Tosefa'a told Ravina to excommunicate him. Ravina objected that a teaching allows one to draw for vegetables in order to eat them. Rabba Tosefa'a answered that the word there does not mean drawing water at all. In the discussion that follows he explains it as thinning out vegetables, and when Ravina cites a teaching that explicitly allows drawing water, he takes back his view.
12.why: A teaching just quoted allows watering vegetables during the intermediate days in order to eat them, but not to improve their looks. The story turns on what the key word in that teaching means.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who defended the man drawing water.

people.name: Rabba Tosefa'a
people.about: A Sage who wanted the man excommunicated.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is allowed and some is not.
To place a person under a ban, cutting him off from the community for a time.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

12.flag: The STORY ends mid-sentence; its continuation and the resolution (Rabba Tosefa'a retracts) are in AFTER segments 5-6.

13.note: Rav Kahana reported, through Rav Yehuda, an incident Rav told: a man saved up money to go up to Jerusalem for a pilgrimage Festival. A professional eulogizer came and stood at the door of his house, and the man's wife took the money and gave it to him. The man then held back and did not go. At that time the Sages ruled that one may not stir up mourning for a dead relative, or eulogize him, in the thirty days before a pilgrimage Festival.
13.why: The mishna forbids lamenting the dead in the thirty days before a Festival, and the Gemara asks why thirty. Rav's story gives one reason, money for the Festival being spent; Shmuel then offers another, that grief lasts thirty days.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose account this is, passed on by Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: He transmitted the account from Rav.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: He reported the account in Rav Yehuda's name.

terms.meaning: Passover, Shavuot or Sukkot, when people went up to the Temple in Jerusalem.
A professional mourner paid to deliver laments for the dead.
Stirring up mourning again for a relative who has died.

14.note: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts, studied the laws of oaths in Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's study hall. They took leave of him in the evening and came back to take leave again in the morning. He asked whether they had not already done so. They said he had taught them that a student who takes leave and then stays the night in the same town must take leave again, learned from two verses on when Solomon sent the people home. Rabbi Shimon told his son that these were men of distinction and he should go to them for a blessing. The son found them puzzling over two verses in Proverbs that seem to contradict each other. What happened when he came to them follows later.
14.why: The Gemara has just been expounding the verses about Solomon dedicating the Temple and sending the people home; the two students draw a rule of conduct from those same verses.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai
people.about: One of two students who took leave of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai twice.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: The other student.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: Their teacher, who sent his son to them for a blessing.

people.name: Solomon
people.about: The king in the verses the students cite.

terms.meaning: A student's formal farewell to his teacher.
The translation's phrase for wise and learned men.

14.flag: Cut mid-episode: the students' answer to their question and the son's encounter with them (the blessing) continue in AFTER and the next story.

15.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's son came to the two Sages, Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda son of converts, and told them his father had sent him for a blessing. They said: may you sow and not reap, bring in and not take out, take out and not bring in; may your house be destroyed and your lodging inhabited, your table be confused, and may you not see a new year. He went home and told his father they had not only failed to bless him but had hurt him. His father asked what they said, then told him these were all blessings: to sow and not reap means to have sons who do not die; to bring in and not take out means to bring brides for your sons and have the sons live; to take out and not bring in means to marry off daughters whose husbands live, so they do not return home.
15.why: This finishes the episode in which Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai sent his son to the two Sages for a blessing. The Gemara then tells a second story of a blessing whose meaning was hidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai
people.about: One of the two Sages who gave the son a blessing that sounded like a curse.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: The other Sage.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: The father, who explained that the words were blessings.

15.flag: Starts mid-episode (the son's errand is set up in the previous story) and stops partway through the father's explanation; the last three blessings are explained in AFTER segments 6-7.

16.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta took leave of Rav, and his father told him to go back for a blessing. Rav said: may it be God's will that you neither shame others nor feel ashamed. At home his father asked what Rav had said, and he answered that it was just words. His father told him Rav had given him the blessing God gave Israel, and God gave it twice, as Joel writes: My people shall never be ashamed, and again, My people shall never be ashamed.
16.why: It follows the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's son, whose blessing sounded like a curse; the Gemara adds another blessing whose weight the one receiving it missed.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta
people.about: He was blessed by Rav and thought it was nothing special.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who gave the blessing.

people.name: God
people.about: His blessing of Israel in Joel is the one Rav repeated.

17.note: Rav Beivai had a daughter and spread lime on her body, one limb at a time, to remove her hair; when he married her off he received four hundred dinars for her. A gentile neighbor who had a daughter spread lime on her all at once, and she died. The neighbor said: Beivai killed my daughter. Rav Naḥman said: Rav Beivai drinks beer, so his daughters need lime; we who do not drink beer, our daughters do not need it.
17.why: The mishna lets women carry on their cosmetic treatments during the intermediate days of a Festival, and the Gemara has been describing how girls removed body hair with lime, flour or oil. This story about lime follows.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: A Sage who treated his daughter with lime, limb by limb.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who said beer drinkers' daughters need such treatment and others' do not.

terms.meaning: A caustic powder that was smeared on the skin to remove hair.
Coins; four hundred was a large sum given at her marriage.

18.note: During the intermediate days of a Festival the Bedita River overflowed and left fish stranded on its banks. Everyone went out, caught fish and brought them home, and Rava permitted them to salt some of them.
18.why: The mishna allows preserving food during the intermediate days only if it can be eaten on the Festival. Abaye challenges Rava's permission on just that ground, and Rava answers that fish which would spoil count as property about to be lost.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who allowed people to salt the fish they caught.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is allowed and some is not.
Food such as pickles or salted fish, prepared to keep for later.

18.flag: Very short; Abaye's challenge to Rava and Rava's reply (and an alternative version of the ruling) in AFTER segments 5-7 read as part of the same incident.

19.note: Maryon son of Ravin and Mar son of Rav Aḥa son of Rava owned a team of oxen together, one ox each. A death struck Mar's family, and he unhitched his ox from the team so no work would be done with it while he mourned. Rav Ashi said: does a great man like Mar behave this way? Even if he does not mind his own loss, does he not mind his partner's? A teaching says animals hired out to others may go on working. The Gemara explains that Mar held that an important person is different.
19.why: A baraita has been setting out what work may be done for a mourner, including that animals hired or leased to others may keep working. Rav Ashi measures Mar's conduct against that rule.

people.name: Maryon, son of Ravin
people.about: Co-owner of the team of oxen.

people.name: Mar, son of Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: Co-owner who, while in mourning, took his ox out of the team.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who criticized Mar for causing his partner a loss.

terms.meaning: A polite way of saying a relative died and he was in mourning.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
A leading figure may hold himself to a stricter standard than the law requires, so others do not take it lightly.

20.note: Gentile contractors built a mansion for Mar Zutra son of Rav Naḥman outside the Sabbath limit. Rav Safra and Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana happened to come there but would not go into it; the translation explains this was because it had been built on the Sabbath. Some say that Mar Zutra himself did not go into it either.
20.why: Shmuel has just ruled that gentile contractors may work for a Jew on the Sabbath outside the Sabbath limit. The Gemara asks why these Sages avoided the house anyway and answers that an important person is different, or that Mar Zutra had supplied the straw for the bricks.

people.name: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage for whom the mansion was built.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage who would not enter the mansion.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana
people.about: A Sage who came with Rav Safra and also stayed out.

terms.meaning: Workers paid for a finished job rather than by the day, who set their own hours.
The distance outside a town, about two thousand cubits, within which one may walk on the Sabbath.
